title: Deep Mutational Scanning of FDX1 Identifies Key Structural Determinants of Lipoylation and Cuproptosis
abstract: Cuproptosis is a recently described form of regulated cell death triggered by ionophore-induced copper (Cu) overload in mitochondria. It is critically dependent on ferredoxin 1 (FDX1), a mitochondrial iron-sulfur cluster containing protein that acts as an electron shuttle. FDX1 reduces ionophore-bound Cu(II) to Cu(I), thereby triggering its release, and promotes mitochondrial protein lipoylation, which is directly targeted by the released copper to drive cell death. Despite the pivotal role of FDX1 in cuproptosis, the structural determinants underlying its distinct functions remain unclear. To address this, we performed deep mutational scanning on FDX1 and find that two conserved solvent-exposed residues, D136 and D139, on alpha helix 3 are essential for both cuproptosis and lipoylation. Charge-reversal mutations at these positions abolish FDX1's ability to induce cuproptosis and support lipoylation in cells, despite retaining full enzymatic activity in vitro. Guided by structural and genomic analyses, we further identify dihydrolipoamide dehydrogenase (DLD), the E3 subunit of lipoylated complexes as an alternative FDX1 reductase both in cells and in vitro. Together, these findings establish the acidic alpha helix 3 of FDX1 as a critical interface for its upstream regulation and suggest that FDX1's roles in cuproptosis and in lipoylation are both structurally and functionally linked.

narrative:
Short impact summary

This Nature Communications article has already seen measurable scholarly uptake, with 21 citations and a field- and year-normalized standing in the top 10% of papers. Its influence is also reflected in downstream reuse: the work has been cited or otherwise reused in 22 documented items, including follow-on research and a review, indicating that the findings are being taken up across the emerging cuproptosis literature.

Full narrative

The article uses deep mutational scanning to map structural features of FDX1 that control lipoylation and cuproptosis, addressing a central mechanistic question in a rapidly developing area of cell death research. Published in 2025 in Nature Communications by a team spanning Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, Pennsylvania State University, and the Broad Institute, it has the profile of a foundational methods-and-mechanism study rather than a narrowly local report.

The citation record suggests that the paper is being used as a reference point for subsequent work on copper biology, regulated cell death, and related cancer mechanisms. The citing literature is concentrated in 2026 and includes articles in venues such as Cells, Cell Chemical Biology, Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology, and International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The thematic spread of those citing works shows that the paper is informing both mechanistic discussions of cuproptosis and broader applications to cancer, metabolism, and trace-element biology.

Several reuse and stewardship signals reinforce that this is an active research asset. The article is open access, has accompanying materials in Figshare, and the project code is available through GitHub, all of which lower barriers to verification and extension. Funding from NSF, NCI, and NIGMS further indicates support for the underlying experimental and computational work, while Europe PMC also records a biomedical article mention.

At the same time, the record is still relatively early in public attention outside the scholarly literature. Event-data sources do not show online mentions, and preprint-related metrics are unavailable in the archive. In other words, the strongest evidence here is academic rather than social: the paper is already functioning as a reference for a fast-moving field, but the broader public-discourse footprint is not captured in the available sources.
